title: Emotional intelligence
note: Evidence-graded emotional skills as one chain: notice, name, reframe, respond, team climate. Each concept is a rule, a model, its traps and one example, with study claims named so you can weigh them. Refresh yearly.

concepts.s: Emotional skill is a chain you can train link by link: notice the signal, name it precisely, reframe it, then respond to people and teams.

x.b:
1. Notice: body signals and the other person's cues.
  2. Name: a precise label lowers intensity.
  3. Reframe: change the meaning before the reaction sets.
  4. Respond: listen, assert, negotiate, give feedback.
  5. Team climate: psychological safety lets the whole team do the same.

This mirrors Joseph and Newman's (2010) meta-analytic cascade: perceiving feeds understanding, which feeds regulation, which feeds performance.
Trap: Treating "EQ" as one score you have or lack. The links are separate skills with separate evidence.
A peer derails your roadmap in a meeting. Notice: jaw tight. Name: "cornered". Reframe: they are under budget pressure. Respond: loop their concern, then state your limit.
After your next charged meeting, write one line per link: noticed, named, reframed, responded. The weakest line is what to train.

cards.q: Your weekly reviews keep going badly and you can't say why. Which link do you train first?
cards.a: Notice and name: log the early body signal and a precise emotion word after each review.

cards.q: Why treat EI as a chain of skills rather than one trait?
cards.a: The links (perceiving, understanding, regulating, responding) are separable, with separate evidence, so you can train the weakest one.

concepts.s: "EI" names three different constructs, and only specific, trainable skills hold up once personality and IQ are controlled for.

x.b:
• Ability EI (Mayer-Salovey, MSCEIT): a test with right answers. Distinct from personality; predicts performance positively in emotionally demanding jobs and negatively in jobs with little emotional labor (Joseph and Newman 2010).
  • Trait EI (Petrides, TEIQue) and mixed EI (Goleman, Bar-On's EQ-i): self-report. Its predictive power is mostly conscientiousness, extraversion, stability, IQ, self-efficacy and self-rated performance restated; controlling for them leaves almost nothing (Joseph et al. 2015).
  • Training raises scores moderately on both ability and mixed measures; published studies report bigger effects than unpublished ones (Mattingly and Kraiger 2019).

Trap: "EQ matters more than IQ." No meta-analysis supports it for job performance.
Trap: Using a self-report EQ test for hiring. It is fakeable and mostly measures personality.
A vendor says EQ predicts leadership. Ask: which stream, which instrument, and was personality controlled? Usually not, so discount it.
Take the last EI claim you read; name the stream, the instrument and what was controlled. If you can't, discount it.

cards.q: In which jobs does tested (ability) EI predict performance best?
cards.a: Jobs high in emotional labor, where managing your own and others' emotions is the work.

cards.q: A workshop raised everyone's EQ self-scores. Why is that weak evidence?
cards.a: Self-ratings right after training partly reflect expectation and demand effects; judge by behavior or outcomes instead.

concepts.s: Putting a feeling into specific words lowers its intensity and points to the right next move.

x.b:
Affect labeling: naming an emotion reduced amygdala response and raised right ventrolateral prefrontal activity (Lieberman et al. 2007); labeling also lowers arousal and distress (Torre and Lieberman 2018).

Granularity (Barrett): people who distinguish "resentful" from "anxious" regulate better (Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight 2015; mostly correlational).

Trap: Venting is not labeling. Rumination sustains emotion; a brief label followed by a decision is the active ingredient.
Trap: Labeling someone else as a verdict ("you're defensive"). Label others tentatively: "sounds frustrating".
"Stressed" leads nowhere. "Resentful my team's work was credited elsewhere" points to one conversation; "anxious about the CIO review" points to preparation.
Three times a day for two weeks, log one specific emotion word, intensity 1-10 and the trigger; ban "stressed" and "fine".

cards.q: Your log says "stressed" every day. What should replace it?
cards.a: A specific word plus its trigger, e.g. "anxious about Thursday's review", because each points to a different action.

cards.q: How do you label another person's emotion without escalating?
cards.a: Tentatively and descriptively ("it sounds frustrating"), never as a diagnosis.

concepts.s: Changing what a situation means beats hiding your reaction, because suppression keeps the feeling and taxes memory and rapport.

x.b:
Gross's process model orders strategies by timing: pick the situation, modify it, shift attention, reappraise, then suppress the response. Earlier is cheaper.

Habitual reappraisers report more positive emotion and better relationships (Gross and John 2003). Suppression impairs memory for what was said during the emotional event (Richards and Gross 2000) and raises partners' blood pressure (Butler et al. 2003). Meta-analysis: reappraisal has a small-to-medium effect; suppression changes expression, not feeling (Webb, Miles and Sheeran 2012).

Trap: Reappraisal as forced positivity. It means an accurate alternative reading, not a comforting lie.
Trap: Saving it for peak arousal. Reappraisal needs spare attention, so plan it before the meeting.
Default read: "the exec is attacking my competence". Plausible alternative: "budget pressure; they need a cheaper option". Situation move: send a pre-read so there are fewer surprises.
Before a contentious meeting, write the threatening reading and the most plausible alternative, plus one move that changes the situation.

cards.q: Before a tense review, which regulation family is cheapest to use?
cards.a: The early ones: situation selection or modification (pre-read, agenda, 1:1), before the emotion starts.

cards.q: What makes a reappraisal valid?
cards.a: It is an accurate, plausible alternative interpretation, not forced positivity.

concepts.s: Under pressure, use your body's early signal as a cue and run a pre-set routine, because judgment degrades once you are flooded.

x.b:
• Early signal: tight jaw, fast speech, heat. People's sense of their body awareness often isn't accurate (Garfinkel et al. 2015), so treat it as a cue to pause, not as evidence.
  • Breathwork, 5 minutes a day, improved mood more than mindfulness in a 108-person trial, with cyclic sighing best (Balban et al. 2023).
  • Self-distancing: self-talk in your own name reduced distress and improved performance (Kross et al. 2014).
  • If-then plans have medium-to-large effects on goal attainment (Gollwitzer and Sheeran 2006).

Trap: Planning around a willpower tank. Large preregistered replications failed to find ego depletion (Hagger et al. 2016).
Trap: "I'm excited" reframing (Brooks 2014): a replication raised felt excitement but not rated performance (Poynter and Pasqualini 2025).
Before: two sighs plus one if-then ("if interrupted, I ask a question first"). If flooded, ask for a break and decide nothing. After: debrief in third person.
For three high-stakes meetings, run the routine and log arousal before and after, and anything you regretted saying.

cards.q: You feel flooded mid-meeting. What is the rule?
cards.a: Ask a question or request a break, and commit to no decisions until you are regulated.

cards.q: Why not plan your day around ego depletion?
cards.a: Large preregistered replications failed to find the effect, though sleep and fatigue still matter.

concepts.n: Empathy: model them, don't absorb them
concepts.s: Cognitive empathy (modeling what someone thinks and needs) wins negotiations and keeps judgment clear, while absorbing their distress burns you out.

x.b:
• Cognitive: perspective-taking. Helped negotiators find deals more than emotional empathy did (Galinsky et al. 2008).
  • Affective: feeling what they feel. Biased toward the near and similar.
  • Compassion: caring and wanting to help. Compassion training raised positive affect; empathic-distress training raised negative affect (Singer and Klimecki 2014).
Trap: Equating empathy with agreement. You can model their position exactly and still push back.
Before a cross-team ask, write their position in their words, their top two pressures, and what a win looks like for their boss. Frame the ask as their win.
Could the other side read your summary of their position and call it fair?
Before a cross-team ask, write their position, top two pressures and their boss's win; check it with someone on their team.

cards.q: A stakeholder is upset and you feel drained after every call. Which empathy mode should you shift to?
cards.a: From affective empathy (absorbing distress) to cognitive empathy plus compassion.

cards.q: Why doesn't empathy require agreement?
cards.a: Modeling someone's view accurately is separate from accepting it; it makes your pushback land better.

concepts.s: Loop for understanding: paraphrase their point and check it before you add yours, because people who feel heard become less defensive and more open.

x.b:
High-quality listening (attention, comprehension, goodwill) makes speakers less anxious and their attitudes less extreme (Kluger and Itzchakov 2022). Active-listening replies made speakers feel more understood than advice did (Weger et al. 2014).

Loop: open question, silence, paraphrase content, reflect feeling tentatively, ask "did I get that right?", and only then give your view (Gary Friedman's term).

Trap: Formulaic paraphrase with no real attention. People detect it, and goodwill carries much of the effect.
Trap: Listening only to reload your rebuttal.
"So the main risk you see is the migration date, and it sounds like you've been burned before. Is that it?" "Yes, exactly." Now propose.
In your next 1:1, give no opinion until you've looped once and heard "yes, exactly".

cards.q: Which listening component do people detect when it's missing from a paraphrase?
cards.a: Genuine attention (goodwill); without it the paraphrase reads as formula.

cards.q: A stakeholder keeps repeating the same complaint. What does that usually signal?
cards.a: They don't feel heard yet: loop their point until they confirm it.

concepts.s: Read people against their own baseline and clusters of cues, then test the read, because single facial expressions do not reliably reveal emotion.

x.b:
A major review found facial configurations do not map reliably to specific emotions across people and contexts (Barrett et al. 2019). Mood spreads through groups and shifts cooperation (Barsade 2002), including yours when you lead.

  • Baseline: compare to their normal.
  • Cluster: several cues together.
  • Context: what just happened, who holds power.
  • Test: "I sense hesitation; what am I missing?"
Trap: Body-language myths (crossed arms = defensive). One cue means little; the room may be cold.
The talkative director goes quiet after the cost slide; the quiet engineer stays quiet. Only the director's silence is signal. Ask them privately.
Mid-meeting, write your read of two people; check one privately afterward. Track your hit rate for a month.

cards.q: Why is a single facial expression weak evidence of emotion?
cards.a: Barrett et al. (2019) found faces don't map reliably to specific emotions across people and contexts.

cards.q: Two people go silent in a meeting. Whose silence is a signal?
cards.a: The one for whom silence departs from their baseline.

concepts.s: State needs and limits directly and specifically, and calibrate with outside feedback, because your own sense of "too much" is unreliable.

x.b:
Assertiveness relates to perceived leadership in an inverted U: too little costs results, too much costs relationships (Ames and Flynn 2007). In the line-crossing illusion, many negotiators seen as appropriately assertive believed they had overstepped, then made needless concessions (Ames and Wazlawek 2014).

DESC script (Bower and Bower): Describe the behavior, Express the concern, Specify the change, state the Consequence. NVC follows the same shape (observation, feeling, need, request); both have thin formal evidence.
Trap: Confusing assertiveness with volume. Calm and specific reads as assertive; loud reads as aggressive.
D: "Scope changed three times last week without a ticket." E: "I'm concerned we'll miss the CIO date." S: "Route changes through intake." C: "Then we can commit to dates."
After your next pushback, ask one attendee where you landed from too soft to too strong; compare with your guess.

cards.q: You worry your pushback was too strong. What do you do instead of apologizing?
cards.a: Ask a trusted attendee where you landed from too soft to too strong; calibrate on their answer.

cards.q: Turn "you always change scope" into the D of DESC.
cards.a: "Scope changed three times last week without a ticket": specific, observable, no judgment.

concepts.s: Keep disagreements about the work from becoming disagreements about each other: regulate first, address emotion before facts, and negotiate on interests with calm, stated limits.

x.b:
• De-escalate: slow down, loop their concern, find the interest behind the position (Fisher and Ury), reframe as a shared problem, move heated threads to a live call.
  • Emotions are information (Van Kleef's EASI model): counterparts concede more to anger they read as signaling limits, but it works less on higher-power counterparts, and anger at the person costs liking and future deals.
  • Anxiety costs money: anxious negotiators open low, exit early and earn less (Brooks and Schweitzer 2011).

Trap: Arguing facts while the other person is flooded. Emotion first, then content.
Trap: Anger as a free tactic with colleagues you'll deal with again.
Before a scope negotiation, write your first ask and walk-away point while calm. In the room: "What's driving the date for you?"
When a thread heats up, stop typing and send: "Let's talk live for ten minutes; I want to understand your concern."

cards.q: A Slack thread is getting heated. What is the first move?
cards.a: Stop replying in text and move to a short live call to understand their concern.

cards.q: When does expressed anger backfire in negotiation?
cards.a: When aimed at the person, or with repeat counterparts: it lowers liking and willingness to deal again.

concepts.s: Aim feedback at the task with high standards and stated belief in the person, and receive it by naming which trigger fired before you respond.

x.b:
Across feedback interventions the average effect was positive, but over a third reduced performance; feedback drawing attention to the self hurt and task-focused feedback helped (Kluger and DeNisi 1996). "Wise feedback" (high standards plus belief you can meet them) raised revision rates (Yeager et al. 2014).

Receiving: Stone and Heen's three triggers are truth, relationship and identity. Name the one that fired, then ask "what would good look like?"
Trap: The feedback sandwich. Praise padding dilutes the message and teaches people to distrust praise.
"I'm flagging the deck's missing cost slide because the bar for CIO reviews is high and I know you can hit it. Add one cost-versus-option table by Friday."
Ask one stakeholder what you could do differently; reply only with thanks and one clarifying question, and note which trigger fired.

cards.q: What share of feedback interventions reduced performance in Kluger and DeNisi (1996)?
cards.a: Over a third; feedback aimed at the self tended to hurt.

cards.q: Feedback stings and you want to argue the facts. What do you do first?
cards.a: Name which trigger fired (truth, relationship, identity), then ask a clarifying question.

concepts.s: Win resources for your team by framing asks in your boss's currency, bringing a recommendation with data, and pre-wiring contentious points one to one.

x.b:
The boss relationship is mutual dependence: know their goals, pressures and preferred style, and your own (Gabarro and Kotter 1980). People stay silent because they overestimate futility and risk; leader openness raises voice (Detert and Burris 2007; Detert and Edmondson 2011).

  • Frame in their currency: risk, cost, speed, credibility.
  • Problem plus recommendation plus the cost of inaction.
  • Pre-wire 1:1 before group meetings; time it for bandwidth.
Trap: Surprising your boss in public, even when right. It spends trust you need for the next ask.
Ask: two more engineers. In their currency: "Without them the CIO dashboard slips a quarter and the audit finding stays open."
Could you write your boss's top three goals and how they like bad news delivered?
Reframe your team's biggest current ask in terms of one of your boss's top goals.

cards.q: Reframe "my team is overloaded" in a boss's currency.
cards.a: State the business cost: e.g. "the audit fix slips a quarter unless we add capacity or drop X".

cards.q: Where should a contentious point first be raised?
cards.a: One to one with the decision-maker (pre-wiring), not by surprise in a group meeting.

concepts.s: A team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks is the best-supported team-level predictor of learning and performance; Edmondson pairs it with high standards.

x.b:
Edmondson (1999): safety predicted learning behavior (asking for help, admitting errors), which predicted performance. Frazier et al.'s (2017) meta-analysis of 136 samples links it to task performance and learning at the group level. Google's Project Aristotle named it the foundation of team effectiveness (observational, Google-only).

Edmondson's framework (a lens, not a tested result): safety plus high standards is the learning zone; safety alone, the comfort zone; standards alone, the anxiety zone.

Trap: Equating safety with niceness. It makes dissent safe; it does not lower the bar.
Trap: Treating it as an individual trait. It is a team-level climate.
Leader moves: frame work as uncertain, admit fallibility ("I'll miss things"), ask "what risk haven't we discussed?", thank the bearer of bad news by name.
At your next team meeting ask "What risk haven't we discussed?", wait through the silence, and thank the first person by name.

cards.q: Through what behavior does psychological safety improve team performance (Edmondson 1999)?
cards.a: Learning behavior: asking for help, admitting errors, seeking feedback.

cards.q: People speak up freely, but missed targets carry no consequence. Which of Edmondson's zones is this?
cards.a: The comfort zone: safety without high standards.

concepts.s: Use Lencioni's five dysfunctions as diagnostic vocabulary on top of Project Aristotle's evidence, knowing the pyramid's ordering is untested.

x.b:
Lencioni's ladder maps onto Aristotle's dynamics: trust and constructive conflict to psychological safety, commitment to structure and clarity, accountability to dependability, results to impact; Aristotle's meaning has no rung. The model comes from a business fable. In a 40-team student study, only inattention to results correlated significantly with performance (Soares et al. 2026).

Durable residue: commitment needs debate first; accountability is peer to peer; a leader's first team is their peers.
Trap: Fixing "trust" with offsites while shared results are unclear. In the one quantitative test (a small student study), results was the only rung tied to performance.
Meetings end in nods, then nothing ships. Diagnosis: no real debate, so no commitment. Fix: ask each person for their objection before deciding.
Before your next decision, ask each person for their strongest objection, then check a week later whether everyone acted on the decision.

cards.q: Which of Lencioni's dysfunctions correlated with team performance in Soares et al. (2026)?
cards.a: Only inattention to results; absence of trust did not.

cards.q: A team agrees in the room, then quietly doesn't follow through. Which rung failed?
cards.a: Commitment, usually because there was no real debate before the decision.
